intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Stickler syndrome type VI (STL6) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL9A3 gene on chromosome 20q13.3.

checks.claim: Stickler syndrome type VI (STL6) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL9A3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we report a new case of a patient with recessive Stickler syndrome caused by novel compound heterozygous mutations in the COL9A3 gene with a more severe phenotype.
checks.explanation: Paper describes recessive STL from homozygous (prior) and compound heterozygous (this case) COL9A3 mutations; STL6 label is OMIM nomenclature.

checks.claim: The COL9A3 gene is located on chromosome 20q13.3.
checks.evidence_quote: The rarest recessive form of STL is caused by mutations in the COL9A3 gene mapped to 20q13.3 loci.

paragraphs.text: Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive collagenopathy caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the COL9A3 gene. Rad et al. (2022) found high myopia and moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss to be consistent features in all reported cases. Skeletal findings, such as epiphyseal or spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, were more variable. Vitreoretinal degeneration, retinal detachment, and cataract occurred in some patients.

checks.claim: Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive collagenopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we report three families with five affected individuals clinically diagnosed with autosomal recessive STL due to biallelic LOF variants in COL9A3.

checks.claim: Stickler syndrome type VI is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the COL9A3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we report three families with five affected individuals clinically diagnosed with autosomal recessive STL due to biallelic LOF variants in COL9A3.

checks.evidence_quote: We find high myopia and moderate-severe hearing loss to be consistent features amongst all cases while skeletal findings seem more variable.

checks.claim: Rad et al. (2022) found moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss to be a consistent feature in all reported cases of COL9A3-related Stickler syndrome.

The sibs also had moderate to severe intellectual disability. Rad et al. (2022) tabulated these patients as Moroccan offspring of first-cousin parents.

paragraphs.text: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) reported a boy whose parents were third cousins from India. He failed his newborn hearing screen. Audiology at 5 months identified moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss on the right and severe sensorineural hearing loss on the left, and the hearing loss remained stable. A head CT at 7 months showed mild enlargement of the vestibular aqueducts. He had no myopia at 5 months, but by 2 years his myopia was -6.75 OD and -8 OS, progressing to -10.75 OD and -11.25 OS by 12 years. No vitreous abnormalities were noted. Femoral and tibial bowing were present at birth. Radiographs at 6 years showed slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, normal knee epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly. Growth parameters and intelligence were normal. He also had autoimmune hypothyroidism, identified at 10 years. His parents and sister were not reported to have hearing loss, myopia, or skeletal anomalies.

paragraphs.text: Nixon et al. (2019) assessed 6 patients from 4 families with recessive Stickler syndrome due to type IX collagen variants. One family, with 2 patients, had a COL9A3 variant. All 6 patients were highly myopic, with congenital megalophthalmos and abnormal, hypoplastic vitreous gel, and all had sensorineural hearing loss. One patient had severe arthropathy. Markova et al. (2021) noted that the eldest COL9A3 patient reported by Nixon et al. (2019) had refraction of up to -23 D in each eye at 20 years of age. That patient also had severe arthropathy and operated scoliosis and used a wheelchair.

paragraphs.text: Markova et al. (2021) reported a boy from a nonconsanguineous family. At 1 month he had adductor spasm, hip dysplasia, and bilateral absence of ossification centers. Congenital high bilateral myopia was found at 3 months. His speech development was delayed, and bilateral grade 3-4 sensorineural hearing loss was diagnosed at 11 months. Spinal radiographs at 1 and 3 years showed sacral spina bifida occulta, mild platyspondyly, and kyphosis with the apex at T11. Radiographs of the lower limbs at 3 years showed flattened and irregular femoral heads, broadened and shortened femoral necks, coxa valga, and flattened distal femoral epiphyses. Ophthalmic assessment showed peripheral pigment rearrangement, multiple vitreous floaters, and a preretinal membrane in the right eye, with a normal electroretinogram. At 2 years 5 months he had valgus knee deformity, waddling gait, rapid fatigability, and pain in the lower limb joints. Facial features included a slightly flattened nasal bridge, small nose, mild midface hypoplasia, and high palate. He also had genu valgum and planovalgus foot deformity. The authors considered the phenotype more severe than in earlier COL9A3 cases because of the early-onset arthropathy and vitreoretinal degeneration.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) reported 5 affected individuals from 3 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families. In family 1, the only affected individual was a 28-year-old woman born to first-cousin parents. She had high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration with empty vitreous, multiple lattice degenerations, and retinal pigmentary changes. She also had severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss. Her joint examination and x-rays were normal, although she complained of knee pain. In family 2, 2 brothers aged 65 and 57 years had a history of multiple vitreoretinal surgeries for recurrent rhegmatogenous retinal detachment caused by advanced vitreoretinal degeneration. The older brother was blind without light perception. Both brothers had severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss and a herniated cervical disc. In family 3, a boy aged 11.8 years and his sister aged 3.1 years had myopia and congenital moderate to severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss. Both had spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, pes planus, depressed nasal bridge, and anteverted nares. None of the patients had intellectual disability. The authors observed that the older patients in family 2 had only myopia, hearing loss, and a herniated cervical disc, whereas the much younger patients in family 3 had more prominent skeletal and craniofacial findings.

agent.process_note: I read all 5 files completely. Three are full texts (Hanson-Kahn 2018, Markova 2021, Rad 2022); Faletra 2014 and Nixon 2019 are abstracts only. Faletra's abstract does not give the number of patients, their ancestry, their clinical details, or the zygosity of the mutation. Those details come from the summaries in Hanson-Kahn and Rad, and the entry says so. Nixon's abstract does not name the COL9A3 variant. The c.1411C>T (p.Arg471Ter) designation is taken from Rad's Table 2. The protein change for c.650dupC is not stated in Hanson-Kahn, and Rad's two tables disagree on it, so I gave only the nucleotide change. Rad gives p.Leu119Serfs*9 in the text and *10 in the table, and I recorded both. No gene MIM number or cytogenetic location was supplied in the reference data. I therefore left out the MIM number and took the 20q13.3 location from Markova.
